entries.meaning: A small animal with six legs, a body in three parts, and usually wings. ---
examples: The porch light pulls in every insect in the neighborhood.
She studies insects that live only in caves.
Not every crawling thing is an insect — spiders have eight legs.

entries.meaning: Any small crawling or flying insect, in everyday speech. ---
examples: There's a bug crawling up the wall behind you.
The screen door keeps most of the bugs out.
Some kind of bug landed in my coffee.
entries.contrast: In casual American English bug covers almost any small creepy-crawly, including spiders — insect is the precise word.

entries.meaning: An insect or animal that damages crops, food, or property. ---
examples: Deer are the worst pest in this garden.
The farm loses about a tenth of its corn to pests.
We hired someone to deal with the pests in the attic.

entries.meaning: Small harmful animals such as rats, mice, and lice, taken as a group. ---
examples: The building was condemned because of vermin.
Those old grain sheds are full of vermin.
Vermin were getting in through a gap under the siding.
entries.contrast: Vermin has no plural -s but takes a plural verb: vermin are, never vermin is.

entries.meaning: An organism that lives on or in another creature and feeds off it. ---
examples: A tapeworm is a parasite that lives in the gut.
The vet tested the puppy for parasites.
Some wasps lay eggs inside caterpillars and live as parasites.

entries.meaning: Any living animal, especially one that seems strange or unfamiliar. ---
examples: Some creature was scratching around under the deck all night.
Tide pools are full of tiny creatures.
It looked like a creature out of a science fiction movie.

entries.meaning: An informal American word for any small animal or insect. ---
examples: Some critter has been digging up the flower beds.
The woods around the cabin are full of critters.
He caught the critter in a jar and let it go outside.

entries.meaning: A small flying insect with two wings that is often found around food and garbage. ---
examples: There's a fly buzzing against the kitchen window.
Close the lid or you'll have flies all over the trash.
He swatted the fly with a rolled-up magazine.

entries.meaning: The common gray fly that gets into kitchens and lands on food. ---
examples: A single housefly can ruin a picnic.
Houseflies were bouncing off the screen all afternoon.
That's just a housefly, not a wasp.

entries.meaning: A large biting fly whose bite is sharply painful. ---
examples: A horsefly got me on the back of the leg.
The horseflies down by the lake are brutal in August.
You feel a horsefly bite immediately.

entries.meaning: A very small flying insect that gathers in clouds near water or fruit. ---
examples: A cloud of gnats hung over the trail.
There's a gnat in my wine glass.
The gnats came out as soon as the sun went down.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: gnat is said exactly like nat, not with a g at the front.

entries.meaning: A tiny two-winged fly that swarms near lakes and streams. ---
examples: Midges were rising off the water at dusk.
A midge flew straight into my eye.
The fish were feeding on midges all evening.

entries.meaning: The soft white legless young of a fly. ---
examples: There were maggots in the bottom of the trash can.
He uses a maggot as bait when he fishes for bluegill.
Meat left out in the heat will be full of maggots by morning.

entries.meaning: The thick pale larva of a beetle, usually found in soil. ---
examples: The lawn died because grubs ate the roots.
I turned over a rock and found a fat white grub.
Skunks dig up the yard looking for grubs.

entries.meaning: A flying insect that gathers nectar from flowers and can sting. ---
examples: A bee landed on the rim of my soda can.
The lavender out front is always covered in bees.
He's allergic, so a bee sting is a real emergency.
entries.contrast: Bee sounds exactly like the verb be — only context tells them apart in speech.

entries.meaning: The kind of bee that people keep in hives to produce honey. ---
examples: A single honeybee visits thousands of flowers a day.
Honeybees pollinate about a third of what we eat.
That's a honeybee, not a wasp — look at the fuzzy body.

entries.meaning: A large round furry bee with a loud low buzz. ---
examples: A bumblebee was bumping against the porch light.
Bumblebees nest in the ground, not in hives.
The bumblebee was so heavy it bent the flower over.

entries.meaning: A slender stinging insect with a narrow waist and a smooth body. ---
examples: A wasp built a nest under the eaves.
Wasps get aggressive around food in late summer.
Unlike a bee, a wasp can sting you more than once.
entries.contrast: Spelled with a but pronounced with the ah of hot: WAHSP, never WASP with the vowel of cat.

entries.meaning: A large aggressive wasp with a powerful sting. ---
examples: A hornet flew in through the open window.
Don't go near that tree — there are hornets in it.
A hornet sting hurts for hours.

entries.meaning: A small black and yellow wasp common around picnics and garbage cans. ---
examples: Yellow jackets were all over the soda cans.
A yellow jacket got into the car on the drive home.
We found a yellow jacket nest in the ground by the shed.
entries.contrast: Americans call this wasp a yellow jacket, not a bee — the mistake matters, because yellow jackets sting repeatedly.

entries.meaning: A structure where a colony of bees lives. ---
examples: He keeps four hives behind the barn.
The whole hive went quiet when it got cold.
Smoke calms the bees before you open the hive.

entries.meaning: A box or natural hollow in which bees live and store honey. ---
examples: There's a wild beehive in that hollow oak.
The city lets residents keep beehives on the roof.
He painted each beehive a different color.

entries.meaning: The wax structure of six-sided cells that bees build to hold honey. ---
examples: She served the bread with a slab of honeycomb.
The honeycomb was heavy with honey.
They cut the honeycombs out and pressed them.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
entries.contrast: The b in comb is silent: the word ends in -kohm, like comb itself.

entries.meaning: Someone who keeps bees for honey or for pollination. ---
examples: A local beekeeper sells honey at the farmers market.
Beekeepers lost a lot of colonies over the winter.
The beekeeper showed us how to lift a frame.

entries.meaning: The wax that bees make and use to build honeycomb. ---
examples: The candles are pure beeswax.
She rubs beeswax into the cutting board.
That lip balm is mostly beeswax and coconut oil.

entries.meaning: An insect or animal that moves pollen from flower to flower. ---
examples: Bees are not the only pollinator in the garden.
They planted wildflowers to bring in pollinators.
Moths are important pollinators at night.

entries.meaning: The sharp part of a bee or wasp that injects venom. ---
examples: Scrape the stinger out with a credit card.
A honeybee leaves its stinger behind and dies.
Wasps have smooth stingers, so they can sting again.
entries.contrast: Americans say stinger for the body part; the British usually call it a sting.

entries.meaning: A painful wound made by a bee, wasp, or scorpion. ---
examples: The sting swelled up by the next morning.
He's had three wasp stings this summer.
A scorpion sting is rarely fatal in this country.
entries.contrast: Bees and wasps sting; mosquitoes and spiders bite. Russian укус covers both, but English never says a bee bite.

entries.meaning: A mark or wound left where an insect or animal has bitten. ---
examples: I woke up with three bites on my ankle.
Don't scratch the bite or it'll get infected.
A spider bite can take weeks to heal.
entries.contrast: Use bite for mosquitoes, spiders, ticks, and snakes, but sting for bees and wasps.

entries.meaning: A small social insect that lives in large underground colonies. ---
examples: There's a line of ants going into the pantry.
One ant can carry many times its own weight.
The ants found the sugar in about ten minutes.
entries.contrast: For most Americans ant sounds exactly like aunt — the word for your parent's sister.

entries.meaning: The mound of dirt an ant colony pushes up over its nest. ---
examples: He stepped right on an anthill in flip-flops.
There are anthills all along the driveway.
The rain flattened the anthill overnight.

entries.meaning: An insect with hard wing covers that meet in a straight line down its back. ---
examples: A shiny green beetle landed on the railing.
Beetles are the largest group of insects on earth.
The beetle rolled onto its back and couldn't get up.

entries.meaning: A small round red beetle with black spots. ---
examples: A ladybug crawled across the back of my hand.
Ladybugs eat aphids, so gardeners love them.
Every fall a few ladybugs get into the house.
entries.contrast: Americans say ladybug; the British say ladybird for the same insect.

entries.meaning: A beetle that flashes light from its abdomen on summer nights. ---
examples: The field was full of fireflies after sunset.
We caught fireflies in a jar and let them go.
I saw the first firefly of the summer last night.
entries.contrast: Much of the American South and Midwest says lightning bug instead of firefly — same insect, different region.

entries.meaning: A small beetle with a long snout that feeds on grain and seeds. ---
examples: There were weevils in the bag of flour.
A single weevil can ruin a whole jar of rice.
Boll weevils wiped out the cotton crop that year.

entries.meaning: A shield-shaped bug that gives off a bad smell when disturbed. ---
examples: Don't squash the stinkbug — you'll regret it.
Stinkbugs come inside as soon as it gets cold.
I vacuumed a stinkbug off the curtain.

entries.meaning: An insect with large colorful wings that flies during the day. ---
examples: A butterfly landed on the edge of the birdbath.
The milkweed brings butterflies into the yard.
She photographed the butterfly before it flew off.

entries.meaning: A dull-colored insect like a butterfly that flies mostly at night. ---
examples: A big brown moth kept hitting the porch light.
Moths got into the wool sweaters in the closet.
The moth left dust on my fingers.
entries.contrast: The plural moths is usually said with a voiced th, like mawthz, not mawths.

entries.meaning: The long soft larva of a butterfly or moth. ---
examples: A fuzzy caterpillar was inching along the fence.
Caterpillars stripped every leaf off the parsley.
The kids kept a caterpillar in a jar until it changed.

entries.meaning: The silk case a caterpillar spins around itself before becoming a moth. ---
examples: There's a cocoon stuck to the underside of the leaf.
The moth came out of its cocoon overnight.
We found two cocoons in the woodpile.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the second syllable, kuh-KOON, not on the first.

entries.meaning: A jumping insect with long back legs that lives in grass. ---
examples: A grasshopper jumped out of the mower's path.
The field was alive with grasshoppers.
He caught a grasshopper to use as bait.

entries.meaning: A small dark jumping insect that chirps loudly at night. ---
examples: A cricket got into the basement and chirped all night.
You could hear crickets through the open window.
The pet store sells crickets to feed to lizards.

entries.meaning: A grasshopper that travels in huge destructive swarms. ---
examples: Locusts ate everything in the fields.
A single locust is harmless; a million of them are not.
The swarm of locusts darkened the sky.

entries.meaning: A large insect that makes a loud buzzing noise on hot summer days. ---
examples: The cicadas were deafening by mid-afternoon.
A cicada shell was stuck to the tree trunk.
This is the year the seventeen-year cicadas come out.
entries.contrast: Americans say sih-KAY-duh; the British say sih-KAH-duh.

entries.meaning: A fast insect with a long thin body and two pairs of clear wings. ---
examples: A blue dragonfly hovered over the pond.
Dragonflies eat mosquitoes by the hundreds.
The dragonfly landed on the tip of the paddle.

entries.meaning: A long green insect that holds its front legs folded as if praying. ---
examples: A mantis was sitting on the screen door.
Mantises will eat almost any insect they can catch.
The praying mantis turned its head to look at me.
entries.contrast: It is a praying mantis, from prayer — not preying, even though the insect does prey on other insects.

entries.meaning: A flat brown insect that lives in buildings and comes out at night. ---
examples: A cockroach ran under the refrigerator when I hit the light.
The apartment had cockroaches in every cabinet.
One cockroach usually means there are many more.

entries.meaning: The everyday American short form of cockroach. ---
examples: The building has a roach problem.
I saw a roach on the counter last night.
They sprayed for roaches twice and it still didn't help.

entries.meaning: A pale soft insect that eats wood and destroys buildings. ---
examples: The inspector found termites in the floor joists.
A termite colony can go undetected for years.
Termite damage isn't covered by the insurance.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, TUR-myt, unlike Russian термит.

entries.meaning: A slim brown insect with a pair of pincers at the end of its body. ---
examples: An earwig fell out of the folded umbrella.
Earwigs hide under flowerpots during the day.
The earwig pinched me, but it barely hurt.

entries.meaning: A small wingless gray insect that lives in damp places like bathrooms. ---
examples: A silverfish darted across the bathroom tile.
Silverfish had eaten the edges of the old books.
We found silverfish behind the baseboards.
entries.contrast: The plural is silverfish, with no -es, exactly like the plural of fish.

entries.meaning: A small flat insect that lives in mattresses and bites people at night. ---
examples: The hotel had to close two floors because of bedbugs.
She checks the mattress seams for bedbugs in every hotel.
A single bedbug in your suitcase is enough to start an infestation.

entries.meaning: A tiny soft insect that sucks sap and covers the stems of plants. ---
examples: The rosebuds are covered in aphids.
Soapy water knocks the aphids off.
One ladybug will eat dozens of aphids a day.

entries.meaning: A tiny jumping insect that lives on animals and feeds on blood. ---
examples: The dog picked up fleas at the kennel.
One flea can jump a hundred times its own length.
We had to treat the carpet for fleas.
entries.contrast: Flea sounds exactly like flee, the verb meaning to run away.

entries.meaning: A small blood-sucking creature that attaches itself to skin and can carry disease. ---
examples: Check the kids for ticks after they come in from the woods.
He pulled a tick off his ankle with tweezers.
Ticks around here carry Lyme disease.
entries.contrast: In American English a checkmark is a check, not a tick — tick is the insect or the sound of a clock.

entries.meaning: A microscopic relative of the tick that lives in dust, bedding, or on plants. ---
examples: Dust mites are the reason her allergies flare up indoors.
The vet found ear mites in both cats.
A single mite is too small to see.
entries.contrast: Mite sounds exactly like might, the modal verb.

entries.meaning: The hard outer shell that supports and protects an insect's body. ---
examples: An insect grows by shedding its exoskeleton.
The empty exoskeleton was still clinging to the bark.
Crabs and beetles both have exoskeletons.

entries.meaning: The middle section of an insect's body, where the legs and wings attach. ---
examples: All six legs come out of the thorax.
The wasp's thorax was banded in yellow.
You can tell the species apart by the markings on their thoraxes.
entries.contrast: Both thoraxes and the Latin plural thoraces are used; thoraxes is the safer everyday choice.

entries.meaning: A creature with eight legs that spins webs and catches insects. ---
examples: There's a spider in the corner of the ceiling.
Most spiders in this country are completely harmless.
She caught the spider in a cup and put it outside.
entries.contrast: A spider is not an insect — it has eight legs and no wings — though English speakers casually call it a bug.

entries.meaning: The net of silk threads a spider spins to catch prey. ---
examples: A web stretched right across the doorway.
The morning dew made the webs visible.
A moth was struggling in the web.

entries.meaning: A spider's web, especially a large or noticeable one. ---
examples: I walked face-first into a spiderweb.
There were spiderwebs in every corner of the shed.
Frost outlined the spiderweb on the window.
entries.contrast: Americans write it as one word, spiderweb; the British normally say spider's web.

entries.meaning: An old dusty spider's web left hanging in a corner. ---
examples: The ceiling was hung with cobwebs.
She swept a cobweb off the light fixture.
Nobody had been in the room for years — cobwebs everywhere.

entries.meaning: A large hairy spider, some kinds of which are kept as pets. ---
examples: His roommate keeps a tarantula in a tank.
A tarantula crossed the road in front of the truck.
Tarantulas look terrifying but rarely bite people.
entries.contrast: The -tula ending is said -chuh-luh, not -too-luh.

entries.meaning: A desert creature with claws and a curved tail that carries a sting. ---
examples: Shake out your boots — scorpions crawl into them.
A scorpion was sitting in the bathtub.
Most scorpions here can hurt you but not kill you.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, SKOR-pee-uhn, unlike Russian скорпион.

entries.meaning: An eight-legged creature such as a spider, tick, mite, or scorpion. ---
examples: Scorpions and spiders are both arachnids.
The exhibit covers insects and arachnids separately.
A tick is an arachnid, not an insect.
entries.contrast: The ch is a hard k sound: uh-RAK-nid.

entries.meaning: A long soft creature with no legs that lives in soil. ---
examples: The rain brought worms out onto the sidewalk.
He cut the worm in half for bait.
Good soil is full of worms.
entries.contrast: Worm and warm differ only in the vowel: WURM has the vowel of bird, WARM the vowel of for.

entries.meaning: The common brown worm that tunnels through garden soil. ---
examples: Earthworms aerate the soil as they dig.
I turned over a shovelful and found a dozen earthworms.
The compost bin is full of earthworms.

entries.meaning: A soft slimy creature like a snail without a shell. ---
examples: Slugs got into the lettuce again.
There was a slug on the back step this morning.
A little salt kills a slug instantly.

entries.meaning: A slow-moving creature that carries a coiled shell on its back. ---
examples: A snail left a silver trail across the patio.
The pond is full of tiny snails.
The kids raced two snails across the sidewalk.

entries.meaning: A long flat creature with one pair of legs on each body segment. ---
examples: A centipede shot across the basement floor.
Centipedes actually hunt other insects.
The bite of a large centipede is painful.

entries.meaning: A slow round-bodied crawler with two pairs of legs on each segment. ---
examples: A millipede curled into a spiral when I touched it.
Millipedes feed on rotting leaves.
We found a millipede under the log.

entries.meaning: A flat worm that attaches to skin and sucks blood. ---
examples: He came out of the pond with a leech on his calf.
Leeches are still used in some kinds of surgery.
Salt makes a leech let go.
entries.contrast: Leech the animal sounds the same as leach, the verb meaning to drain away through soil.

entries.meaning: The presence of pests in large, damaging numbers. ---
examples: The restaurant was closed for a roach infestation.
Infestations usually start in one small corner.
They caught the termite infestation early.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to kill insects and other pests in buildings. ---
examples: The landlord finally sent an exterminator.
Exterminators charge more for a whole-house treatment.
The exterminator said it would take two visits.
entries.русский: дезинсектор, специалист по борьбе с вредителями

entries.meaning: A chemical made specifically to kill insects. ---
examples: The insecticide killed the ants but not the eggs.
New insecticides are harder on bees than people realize.
Don't use insecticide indoors without opening a window.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A cold-blooded scaly animal such as a snake, lizard, or turtle. ---
examples: A turtle is a reptile, not an amphibian.
The zoo's reptile house is kept warm year-round.
Reptiles need an outside heat source to stay active.

entries.meaning: A long legless reptile that moves by sliding along the ground. ---
examples: A snake crossed the trail right in front of us.
Most snakes around here are not venomous.
He grabbed the rake and moved the snake off the porch.

entries.meaning: A formal or literary word for a snake, especially a large or symbolic one. ---
examples: The temple wall was carved with a coiled serpent.
In the story the serpent speaks.
Sea serpents show up in a lot of old sailors' tales.

entries.meaning: A small scaly reptile with four legs and a long tail. ---
examples: A lizard was sunning itself on the wall.
Lizards dart away the second you move.
The lizard dropped its tail and got away.

entries.meaning: A small lizard with sticky feet that can climb glass and walls. ---
examples: A gecko was stuck to the ceiling above the bed.
Geckos eat the mosquitoes that get inside.
The gecko chirped in the middle of the night.

entries.meaning: A large tropical lizard with a ridge of spines down its back. ---
examples: An iguana was sitting in the middle of the road.
Iguanas have taken over parts of South Florida.
The iguana is bigger than the cat.
entries.contrast: The gua is said gwah in one syllable: ih-GWAH-nuh, not ih-goo-AH-nuh.

entries.meaning: A lizard that can change the color of its skin. ---
examples: The chameleon turned nearly black when it got cold.
Chameleons move one slow step at a time.
Each eye of a chameleon moves on its own.
entries.contrast: The ch is a k sound: kuh-MEE-lee-uhn.

entries.meaning: A reptile with a hard shell that covers its body. ---
examples: A turtle was sitting in the middle of the road.
We watched sea turtles come up the beach at night.
The turtle pulled its head into its shell.
entries.contrast: In American English turtle covers land and water species alike; British English reserves turtle for sea species and says tortoise on land.

entries.meaning: A land turtle with a high domed shell that lives a very long time. ---
examples: The desert tortoise is a protected species.
That tortoise is older than my grandfather.
Tortoises eat mostly grass and leaves.
entries.contrast: Spelled -oise but pronounced -tuhs: TOR-tuhs, never tor-TOYZ.

entries.meaning: A large reptile with a long jaw and heavy scales that lives in rivers. ---
examples: A crocodile slid off the bank into the water.
Crocodiles can hold their breath for an hour.
The guide pointed out a crocodile we would never have seen.

entries.meaning: A broad-snouted relative of the crocodile found in the American South. ---
examples: There's an alligator in almost every pond down there.
Alligators sometimes wander onto golf courses.
The alligator didn't move the whole time we watched.

entries.meaning: A large non-venomous snake that kills by squeezing its prey. ---
examples: The pet store had a python almost eight feet long.
Pythons have spread through the Everglades.
A python can go weeks without eating.
entries.contrast: Americans give the second syllable a full vowel, PY-thahn; the British reduce it to PY-thuhn.

entries.meaning: A venomous snake that spreads the skin of its neck into a hood. ---
examples: The cobra raised up and spread its hood.
Cobras are responsible for thousands of deaths a year.
He keeps a cobra behind two locked doors.

entries.meaning: A venomous American snake that shakes a noisy rattle on its tail. ---
examples: We heard the rattlesnake before we saw it.
Rattlesnakes come out to warm up on the rocks.
A rattlesnake bite needs a hospital, not a first-aid kit.

entries.meaning: A venomous snake with long hinged fangs and a triangular head. ---
examples: A pit viper struck at the boot and missed.
Vipers have the longest fangs of any snake.
The viper was coiled under the rock.

entries.meaning: A small venomous snake of Europe and parts of Africa. ---
examples: The only venomous snake in Britain is the adder.
Adders bask on open heath in the morning.
He nearly stepped on an adder in the grass.
entries.contrast: Adder is mainly a British word; Americans say rattlesnake, copperhead, or just viper.

entries.meaning: A heavy tropical snake that wraps around its prey and crushes it. ---
examples: His brother keeps a boa in the garage.
Boas give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
The boa wrapped itself around the branch.

entries.meaning: A very large South American snake that lives in and near water. ---
examples: The anaconda is the heaviest snake in the world.
Anacondas spend most of their time in swamps.
They filmed an anaconda swallowing a caiman.

entries.meaning: A venomous North American snake with a coppery head and banded body. ---
examples: A copperhead was lying in the leaf litter.
Copperheads bite more people here than any other snake.
The copperhead blended right into the mulch.

entries.meaning: A small striped harmless snake common in North American yards. ---
examples: It's just a garter snake — completely harmless.
Garter snakes live under the woodpile every summer.
The kids found a garter snake by the compost.
entries.contrast: The name is garter, like the elastic band, though plenty of Americans mishear it as garden snake.

entries.meaning: The poison that a snake, spider, or scorpion injects with a bite or sting. ---
examples: The venom attacks the blood, not the nerves.
They milk the snakes for venom to make antivenom.
Only a small amount of venom got into the wound.
entries.contrast: Venom is injected by a bite or sting, so the animal is venomous; poison is swallowed or absorbed, so a poisonous mushroom is a different idea entirely.

entries.meaning: A medicine that counteracts the venom of a snake or other animal. ---
examples: The hospital had to fly in antivenom from Phoenix.
Different antivenoms work on different species.
He got the antivenom within an hour of the bite.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A wound caused by a snake's bite. ---
examples: Most snakebites happen when someone tries to move the snake.
The clinic treats a dozen snakebites every summer.
Don't cut a snakebite open — just get to a hospital.

entries.meaning: An animal such as a frog or newt that lives both in water and on land. ---
examples: Frogs, toads, and salamanders are all amphibians.
Amphibians are disappearing faster than any other group.
An amphibian breathes partly through its skin.

entries.meaning: A small smooth-skinned amphibian with long back legs for jumping. ---
examples: A frog jumped off the dock as we walked up.
The frogs start calling as soon as it gets dark.
There was a tiny green frog on the window screen.

entries.meaning: A large frog with a deep booming call. ---
examples: A bullfrog was croaking down by the creek.
Bullfrogs will eat anything they can fit in their mouths.
That bullfrog was the size of my hand.

entries.meaning: A frog-like amphibian with dry bumpy skin that lives mostly on land. ---
examples: A fat toad sat under the porch light eating bugs.
Toads don't actually give you warts.
We moved the toad out of the driveway.
entries.contrast: Toad sounds exactly like towed, the past tense of tow.

entries.meaning: The young of a frog or toad, which lives in water and has a tail. ---
examples: The pond is full of tadpoles in April.
Each tadpole grows back legs first.
We kept tadpoles in a bucket until they turned into frogs.

entries.meaning: A small amphibian like a lizard that spends much of its life in water. ---
examples: There was an orange newt crossing the wet trail.
Newts return to the same pond to breed.
The newt has skin you should not touch and then rub your eyes.
entries.contrast: Americans say NOOT; the British say NYOOT with a y sound after the n.

entries.meaning: A slender amphibian with smooth moist skin and a long tail. ---
examples: We found a salamander under a rotting log.
Salamanders can regrow a lost limb.
The salamander slipped back into the leaves.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, SAL-uh-man-dur, unlike Russian саламандра.

entries.meaning: A substance you put on skin or clothes to keep insects away. ---
examples: Put on some repellent before we go down to the lake.
The strongest repellents contain DEET.
This repellent smells terrible but it works.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: The everyday American name for insect repellent or insect killer in a can. ---
examples: Grab the bug spray off the shelf by the door.
We went through two cans of bug spray that week.
The bug sprays at the drugstore are all about the same.
entries.countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance

entries.meaning: A glass tank set up for keeping reptiles, amphibians, or plants. ---
examples: The gecko lives in a terrarium on his desk.
Terrariums need a heat lamp at one end.
She built a little terrarium out of an old fish tank.

entries.meaning: Coloring or shape that lets an animal blend into its surroundings. ---
examples: The moth's camouflage makes it invisible on bark.
That lizard relies entirely on camouflage.
Snow gives the hare perfect camouflage in winter.
entries.contrast: The ending is said -flahzh, with the soft zh of measure, not -flayj.

entries.meaning: The deep winter sleep some animals fall into to survive the cold. ---
examples: The turtles go into hibernation at the bottom of the pond.
Snakes come out of hibernation in early spring.
Hibernation slows the heart down to a few beats a minute.

entries.meaning: A scientist who studies insects. ---
examples: She trained as an entomologist and now works for the state.
Entomologists identified the beetle from a photo.
The county keeps an entomologist on staff.
entries.contrast: An entomologist studies insects; an etymologist studies word origins — one letter apart, completely different jobs.

entries.meaning: A small white ball of chemical put in stored clothes to keep moths away. ---
examples: The closet smelled like mothballs.
She tucked a mothball into each box of wool.
Grandma's coats always came out of storage smelling of mothballs.

entries.meaning: A flat plastic paddle on a wire handle used for killing flies. ---
examples: The flyswatter is hanging by the back door.
He got it on the first swing with the flyswatter.
We keep two flyswatters in the kitchen all summer.

entries.meaning: A delicate winged insect that hatches in huge numbers and lives only a day or two. ---
examples: Mayflies covered the bridge lights that night.
A mayfly has no working mouth at all.
The trout were rising for mayflies at dusk.

entries.meaning: A smooth shiny lizard with short legs and a long tapering tail. ---
examples: A blue-tailed skink ran along the top of the wall.
Skinks are all over the woodpile in July.
The skink slipped into a crack in the stone.

entries.meaning: A tiny reddish mite larva whose bite leaves an intensely itchy welt. ---
examples: He picked up chiggers walking through the tall grass.
A chigger bite itches for a week.
Chiggers are worst around the ankles and waistband.

entries.meaning: A large green insect like a grasshopper that calls loudly from trees at night. ---
examples: The katydids started up as soon as it got dark.
A katydid looks exactly like a leaf.
You can hear katydids through the screen all August.

entries.meaning: A young insect that looks like a small wingless version of the adult. ---
examples: A dragonfly nymph lives underwater for a year or more.
Cicada nymphs feed on roots in the dark.
The nymph climbed out of the water and split open.

entries.meaning: A wingless insect larva that gives off a steady greenish light. ---
examples: The bank of the stream was dotted with glowworms.
A glowworm glows without flashing.
Glowworms light up the ceiling of that cave.

entries.meaning: The caterpillar of a moth whose cocoon is unwound to make silk. ---
examples: Silkworms eat nothing but mulberry leaves.
One silkworm cocoon yields a single unbroken thread.
The class raised silkworms as a science project.

entries.meaning: A large ocean turtle with flippers instead of legs.
examples: A sea turtle surfaced right next to the boat.
Sea turtles come back to the beach where they hatched.
Volunteers marked the sea turtle nests with stakes.
